v.q: A bank wants to split its monolith. What is the best basis for the service boundaries?
o: Business capabilities and bounded contexts, such as accounts and payments
Technical layers, with one service each for web, logic and data
One service for every database table
The size of the Java packages in the monolith
v.w: Services should be vertical slices of a business capability. Splitting by layer or by table forces every feature to cross many services.

v.q: Which split gives the best service boundaries?
o: By business capability
By technical layer
By database table
By Java package
v.w: Services should own a business capability, such as accounts or payments, so they can change independently.

v.q: What does a bounded context mean in domain-driven design?
o: The area where a term has one precise meaning and model
A limit on how many requests a service accepts
A transaction that spans several services
The set of classes that share one database table
v.w: The word Customer can mean a verified identity in Accounts and a cardholder in Cards. Each context keeps its own model.

v.q: Which statement about a bounded context is NOT true?
o: One model must fit the whole company
A term has one meaning inside it
Different contexts can model the same thing differently
It often maps to a service
v.w: DDD accepts that the word customer can mean different things in different contexts.

v.q: What is the first step of the strangler fig migration?
o: Put a facade such as a gateway in front of the monolith
Rewrite the whole monolith in a new codebase
Split the shared database into one per service
Turn off the monolith for a weekend and switch over
v.w: The facade first forwards everything, so nothing changes for users. Slices are then moved behind it one at a time and each step can be rolled back.

v.q: Which is NOT part of a strangler fig migration?
o: A weekend big-bang cutover
A facade in front of the monolith
Moving one slice at a time
Routing calls to new services
v.w: The approach replaces the old system gradually without a switch-off weekend.

v.q: Which sign best shows a distributed monolith?
o: Services share one database and have to be deployed together
Every service has its own team and its own database
Services communicate mainly through published events
Each service can be released without the others
v.w: It has the operational cost of microservices without independent deployment. The test is whether a service can be changed and released alone.

v.q: Which situation signals a distributed monolith?
o: Several services must be released together
Teams release independently
Each service owns its data
Services communicate through events
v.w: Network calls without independence give the cost of both styles.

v.q: Why consider a modular monolith before microservices?
o: It gives enforced boundaries without network calls
It removes the need to test the module boundaries
It is always faster than any other architecture style
It lets every module write to any table
v.w: Boundaries inside one deployable are cheap to fix. If a module later needs to scale or deploy alone, extraction is mostly mechanical.

v.q: Which statement about a modular monolith is NOT true?
o: Modules may read any table directly
It is deployed as one unit
Module boundaries are enforced
It can become services later
v.w: The point is enforced boundaries, so no module reaches into another module tables.

v.q: In what order should the database be split when extracting a service?
o: Stop direct table access, replicate data through events, then split the schema
Split the database first, then change the code
Copy every table into every service permanently
Keep one shared schema and add cross-service foreign keys
v.w: Do the database last and in reversible steps. Consumers first use an API, then a local copy fed by events or change data capture, then the schema is separated.

v.q: Which step comes first when taking a table away from the monolith?
o: Stop other code reading it directly
Drop the old table
Copy it into every service
Add cross-service foreign keys
v.w: Access goes through an API or events first, and only then is the schema moved.

v.q: What does an anti-corruption layer do?
o: Translates another system's model into your own so it does not leak in
Encrypts all traffic between two services
Retries failed calls with exponential backoff
Stores a copy of every event in an archive
v.w: All translation of codes and formats lives in one adapter, so a change in the other system affects only that layer.

v.q: Which situation calls for an anti-corruption layer?
o: A legacy model leaking in
Encrypting service traffic
Retrying failed calls
Archiving events
v.w: The layer translates the legacy model so its terms do not leak into your domain.

v.q: Which capability is usually the best first candidate to extract as a service?
o: A low-risk edge capability with clear boundaries, such as notifications
The core ledger that every other part depends on
The part of the code nobody understands
The shared utility library used by all modules
v.w: Start where risk is low so the team can build and learn the platform. The most entangled core domain goes last, if it ever needs to move.

v.q: Which capability is a poor first choice to extract?
o: The core ledger every part depends on
Notifications
PDF statement generation
An edge reporting feature
v.w: Start with low-risk pieces that have clear boundaries and learn before touching the core.
